title: Losing Belly Fat Saved Brains for a Decade. Losing Weight Did Not. Why South Asians Cannot Ignore This Study.
excerpt: A 16-year MRI study of 533 adults found that visceral fat — not body weight — drives brain shrinkage. South Asians carry more of it than almost any other group.
body:
The scale is lying to you. A landmark study published in Nature Communications has found that sustained reductions in visceral abdominal fat — the deep fat wrapping around your organs — preserved brain structure and cognitive function over more than a decade. Overall weight loss, by contrast, showed no such protective effect.

For South Asians, who are genetically predisposed to carry disproportionately high levels of visceral fat even at normal body weights, the implications are profound.

## The Longest Study of Its Kind

Researchers led by Professor Iris Shai of Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, in collaboration with Harvard University, Leipzig University and Tulane University, followed 533 women and men in late midlife for 5 to 16 years. All had previously participated in four major dietary clinical trials: DIRECT, CASCADE, CENTRAL and DIRECT-PLUS.

Using repeated MRI scans of both the brain and abdomen, the team tracked how changes in visceral fat over time corresponded to changes in brain structure and cognitive performance.

The findings were unequivocal. Lower accumulation of visceral fat was associated with higher scores on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), preservation of total brain volume and grey matter volume, and a higher Hippocampal Occupancy Score — a sensitive marker of brain ageing and memory. Participants who kept visceral fat low also showed slower enlargement of brain ventricles, a well-established indicator of brain atrophy.

## Weight Is the Wrong Target

Here is the part that upends conventional thinking: these associations were specific to visceral fat. Subcutaneous fat — the pinchable fat under the skin — showed no link to brain outcomes. Neither did BMI, the blunt instrument that most doctors still use to assess metabolic risk.

"Weight alone is not a sensitive marker of the profound metabolic changes occurring in the body," said Dr Dafna Pachter, the study's first author. "Even when weight loss is modest, sustained reductions in visceral fat are associated with preservation of brain structure and a slower rate of atrophy."

Moreover, reductions in visceral fat during an initial 18-month dietary intervention predicted better brain outcomes 5 and 10 years later — even after participants had regained some weight. What mattered was not the number on the scale but where the fat was stored.

## The Glucose Connection

The study identified the biological pathway linking belly fat to brain decay: glucose metabolism. Fasting blood sugar and HbA1c levels were the only biomarkers that predicted the rate of structural brain change over time. Blood lipids and inflammatory markers, which are often blamed for cognitive decline, showed no similar association.

In other words, visceral fat drives brain ageing primarily by wrecking glucose control and insulin sensitivity — which in turn impairs blood flow to the brain, compromises the blood-brain barrier and accelerates grey matter loss.

## Why South Asians Are Especially Vulnerable

South Asians are sometimes described as "thin on the outside, fat on the inside." Multiple studies have shown that people of South Asian descent accumulate more visceral fat relative to their body weight than almost any other ethnic group. A South Asian man with a BMI of 23 — classified as "normal" — may carry as much visceral fat as a Caucasian man with a BMI of 30.

This metabolic phenotype helps explain a persistent puzzle: why do South Asians develop Type 2 diabetes, heart disease and metabolic syndrome at younger ages and lower body weights than other populations? The new brain data adds cognitive decline and dementia to that list.

For NRIs in their 40s and 50s — the age group where this study's participants showed the strongest effects — the message is personal. Standard weight management advice ("lose 10 kilograms") may be missing the point entirely. What matters is targeting the fat you cannot see.

## What Actually Works

The clinical trials underlying this study tested Mediterranean, low-carbohydrate and traditional low-fat diets combined with physical activity. All three reduced visceral fat, but the Mediterranean and low-carb approaches showed stronger and more durable effects on abdominal fat specifically.

Professor Shai summed it up: "The findings point to glucose control and reduction of visceral abdominal fat as measurable, modifiable and achievable targets in midlife — with real potential to slow brain degeneration and reduce the risk of cognitive decline."

For South Asians, the practical takeaway is clear: stop fixating on weight. Get your waist circumference measured. Ask your doctor about an HbA1c test. And if you are carrying fat around your middle, prioritise reducing it — even if the scale barely moves. Your brain, a decade from now, will thank you.

*Sources: Nature Communications, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Circulation*
